description: Multidisciplinary team looking to tackle interesting challenges for humanity in space!
summary:
HAL2030 helps astronauts monitor their health and decide what to check next when help from Earth is delayed, in all future human space exploration missions. One crew dashboard combines wearable readings, personal check-ins, and self-test results so the crew can see who needs attention and what changed.

Routine checks. For example, a built-in guided near-vision test can record results for each eye to help track vision changes associated with spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS). Additionally if an astronaut logs less than six hours of sleep in the past 24 hours and is approaching docking, the app can suggest a three-minute vigilance test (PVT) and compare the result with their personal baseline when available. 

Emergency response. When a reading crosses an alert threshold, the app highlights the affected astronaut and displays a response checklist. A proposed kit locator would show where emergency supplies are stored and light up the right bay. Future plans include a predictive module, that fuses current data and trends to predict or warn against possible health incidents.

Human connection. If private check-ins show sustained low mood or high stress, the app can offer an optional message from home. For new messages over a limited-bandwidth link, we send audio and facial motion. LivePortrait reconstructs the video using a photo and model already on board. Our 4.4-second example used 33 kB versus 310 kB for the original H.264 file.
details:
We built HAL2030 to help astronauts look after their health throughout a mission. It brings routine monitoring, guided self-tests, and response checklists into one app so the crew can see what changed and decide what to check next.

The HAL2030 prototype runs on Python and FastAPI. We use pandas to load recorded and simulated data, SciPy to filter ECG and pulse signals and detect beats, and NumPy to calculate measures such as heart-rate variability. This lets the crew review trends alongside alerts and prewritten recommendations.

The repository includes NASA’s Inspiration4 datasets (OSD-569 and OSD-575) as research references. We use NASA’s May 2024 DONKI solar particle records to ground the simulated radiation scenarios in real space-weather events. Inspiration4 datasets · NASA DONKI

NASA’s ISS wearable research informed which signals we display. Its SANS guidance informed our per-eye near vision check, and its guidance on private psychological conferences informed our mood and stress check-ins. ISS wearable research · SANS technical brief · NASA medical operations

We designed for limited onboard computing, uneven access to specialized equipment, and an intermittent link to Earth. The vision and vigilance checks use a standard display and input controls. The dashboard marks missing sensor readings as unavailable. Local rules select prewritten recommendations. For example, a crew member who logs less than six hours of sleep in the past 24 hours and is approaching docking can get a prompt for a three-minute vigilance test. A vital-sign alert brings up a response checklist, and a proposed kit locator would light up the bay holding the relevant supplies. When the Earth link is available, a future version could send crew approved context to an Earth hosted language model for non urgent questions or summaries.

Limited bandwidth also shapes how crews stay connected with home. In our family message demo, we send audio and facial motion over a simulated Earth Mars link. LivePortrait reconstructs the video locally on a CPU using a preloaded photo and model. The 4.4 second example took 33 kB to send, 89% less data than the original 310 kB H.264 file.
